We have briefly discussed elsewhere (Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 7–12) the difference between, on the one hand, ’odhrîte love, which embodies the ideal of Platonic love and is celebrated in Ibn Dâwûd Ispahânî’s masterpiece, the Kitâb al-Zahra (d. 297/909), and, on the other, the theophanic love experienced by Rûzbehân. Compare (ibid., p. 10) Ibn Dâwûd’s lived understanding of the hadith of the “martyrs of love,” which he followed even to death. Wherever the dominant theme of theophany is missing, the “esoteric meaning” of love and the contemplation of a beautiful being is missing too. Without that theme, love—Eros—cannot take on the essential role of initiation into theophany that Rûzbehân’s spirituality gives it. The difference appears equally clearly in Rûzbehân’s understanding of Majnûn (see below, Chapter VI, § 6, and p. 138, note 200). Of course, mystical meaning does not exclude a collapse that may end in physical death. Popular preachers sometimes sent their devout listeners into trances by speaking about the divinity as they did, using the feminine names of heroines from Arabic courtly poetry (see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, p. 275, note 322, and above, p. 75, note 72). In the Jasmin, Chapter X, § 118, Rûzbehân relates, on the authority of Yûsof Hoseyn Râzî, an account of a gathering at which the celebrated master Zû’l-Nûn Misrî spoke of the love of God. Eleven people died. When the gathering was nearly over, a kind of wanderer stood up: “O Abû’l-Fayz,” he said, “you have spoken enough of love for the Creator. Tell us something now about the love of one creature for another.” Zû’l-Nûn cried out, tore his robe, and fell prostrate. His face became crimson as he murmured in Arabic: “Their pledges have not been released, and their eyes know only tears.” ↩

Jasmin, Chapter IV, § 53. “In saying, ‘Whoever loves and remains chaste ...’, the Prophet knows perfectly well that when the soul looks by the light of the Intelligence, it ceases to be intoxicated by the vapours of sensual nature. He therefore prescribed to the intelligence the training of chaste conduct. Otherwise, the soul’s ship cannot escape the reef of fleshly appetites, because love, by its very nature, sets the whole person in motion, stirring every part.” ↩

Ibid., § 54. “As for the secret kept hidden (ketmân), as indicated by the prince of the Faithful in Love (the Prophet), this concerns the dying down of the soul’s blaze, when the soul has been wholly consumed by the fire of Love and the fierceness of that fire at last subsides. If the lover knocks at Love’s door, he deserves the name of martyr (shahîd) on condition that, wounded in the dwelling of trial by the sword of exclusive devotion, he lets himself be entirely consumed by the fire of Love while keeping his secret. The Prophet also said: Whoever dies consumed by the fire of Love dies a martyr.” See also below, Chapter VI, § 6, and p. 141, note 203. Jasmin, Chapter XIII, § 146. Elsewhere, in an allusion to his spiritual autobiography, Rûzbehân reveals how he in turn lived through Abraham’s experience and entered the same spiritual state: “Like Abraham, deciphering the mystery of the kingdom of the stars, this Sufi [Rûzbehân] also contemplated omnipotence in the act it performs, as one contemplates a bride in a mirror. Having been initiated into this summit, the pedestal of the visible human form, this spirit, newly taught the eternal pre-existence of beauty within love, necessarily emerged as from a cave—from the eye that sees only the outer human form—and made the unknown Signs into signs pointing to the eternal Bride. He too cried out: ‘This is my Lord’ (6:76–78)” (Jasmin, Chapter XIV, § 154). ↩

It is here that the commentator distinguishes three mirrors in which the divine Invisible, God’s visible Form, and the eternal divine Face may respectively be contemplated. Abraham contemplated the first; the power to contemplate the other two was reserved for Muhammad. A translation of this Gloss appears below, in the passage connected with note 111. In Chapter XXIX, § 262, Rûzbehân examines the same theme in relation to mystical states: the state of certain lucidity (sahw), which can grasp the ambiguity of appearance; the state of spiritual intoxication (sokr); and the state in which the ego is effaced (mahw), which combines the previous two and is spiritual intoxication multiplied by itself (sokr dar sokr). Abraham experienced the first state when he prayed: “Lord, show me how you raise the dead” (2:262). Moses experienced the second when he cried: “Lord, show yourself to me, so that I may contemplate you” (7:139), expressing his desire for an absolute vision. Muhammad, finally, was granted both mystical states at once. In the first he asked, “Show me things as they are.” In the second he declared, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” “For God came from Sinai” (the place of Moses’ theophany); “he rose from Seir” (the place of Jesus’ theophany); “and his light shone forth from Mount Paran” (at Mecca, the place of Muhammad’s theophany, as the Seal of the Prophets) (compare Deuteronomy 33:2–3). Compare also Chapter V, § 60, on the difference between Abraham and Joseph. When Abraham saw the stars, he exclaimed, “This is my Lord.” With Joseph it was the reverse: the stars (the eleven stars) acknowledged him as their Lord (12:4), just as the angels prostrated themselves before the beauty of the heavenly Adam. ↩

Jasmin, Chapter VI, § 94, ends as follows: “At whatever level of being Eros appears, whether as love of sensible things or of spiritual realities, love in itself deserves nothing but praise. For physical love is the path leading to spiritual love, and spiritual love the path leading to divine love. Only this mount can carry the burdens of divine love, and only from this cup of allegiance may one taste the drink of purity, which is archetypal Beauty in its pure state. These three essences [human, spiritual, and divine love] are in perpetual movement toward the primordial Source.” ↩

Ibid., § 96. Gloss 62 develops the alchemical comparison: “The mixture must be complete and perfect. Otherwise, the operation merely brings about an apparent change in the form of copper, without reaching the reality of gold. If love has been purified of physical love, a state of divine sacredness spreads throughout the mystical lover’s person. In the mirror of a created being, the lover then attains the direct, eyewitness vision (shohûd) of God and the contemplation of the uncreated Face. But if a trace of natural love remains, the lover will certainly undergo an outward change and stand apart from others by certain qualities; yet there will be no direct vision, nor will the perfection of the human condition (insânîyat) be attained.” ↩

Jasmin, Chapter X, § 122 and Gloss 155; see also above, p. 57, note 47, and p. 86, note 91. Rûzbehân’s allusion to zend and pâzend belongs entirely to the tradition of “closed language” characteristic of Iranian Sufism. His anonymous follower and commentator expands it in this way: “The fire of Beauty blazing upon your face is the radiance of the Burning Bush; and I, a new Moses beholding this theophany, hear the secret meaning of these words: ‘It is I who am God’ (Qur’an 28:30).” The commentator is thereby practising ta’wîl, a spiritual interpretation of symbols that “leads back” the outward appearance of the religion of Fire (âtesh-parastî) to its inner meaning: the worship of Beauty (jamâl-parastî). Whether Sufis or orthodox believers, everyone in Islam knows that the ancient Iranians used the terms zend and pâzend for commentary on their sacred book, the Avesta. Zend and pâzend are thus equated with ta’wîl. Hence the name zendîq applied to anyone who insists upon the necessity and practice of ta’wîl. Yet this was the scriptural foundation of Shiism and, after it, of Sufism. Every outward statement or appearance (both how something looks and how it appears) presupposes an esoteric meaning. To those who understand religion only outwardly, this claim seemed to destroy the very letter of Revelation. Without troubling over distinctions, therefore, they described Shia Muslims, Ismailis, and Sufis as “survivors of the Mazdean Magi within Islam” (Hujwîrî). Iranian Sufis, meanwhile, practised with equal enthusiasm a symbolic “closed language,” with key expressions such as sons of Magi, priest of the Magi, wine of the Magi, Fire Temple, and so on. It was probably within such spiritual circles that the hadith quoted earlier (Book II, Chapter VII, § 3) arose: “Never speak ill of Zoroaster, for Zoroaster was the prophet sent to Iran by the Lord of love” (see our introduction to Moh. Mo’in’s Le Mazdéisme et son influence dans la littérature persane, Tehran, 1948, p. 36; also everything said here about Xvarnah in Suhrawardî’s doctrine, above, Book II, Chapters III and IV). This gives rise to the idea already noted (p. 86, note 91), and still needing fuller examination: in practising ta’wîl, one follows the example of the Zoroastrian religion, and by applying ta’wîl to that religion itself—interpreting the worship of Fire as a symbol of the religion of love—one escapes two related dangers: idolatry and belief in incarnation, anthropomorphism (tashbîh) and abstract monotheism (ta’til). Rûzbehân is constantly on guard against precisely these dangers, into which those who accuse his Sufism of them themselves fall. What the religion of the Magi symbolizes through its dualism, and what forms the basis of its interpretation (ta’wîl) in Sufism (see Latîfa-ye ghaybîya, Moh. Dârâb’s commentary on Hâfez), is both the duality of Lover and Beloved and the apparent duality of the earthly and heavenly Beloved. Both dualities must be led back to the unity of the esoteric tawhîd. In either case, to perceive duality as calling for ta’wîl is to be initiated into theophanic perception: the theophanic contemplation in which the shâhid (contemplating witness) becomes the mashhûd (one contemplated). The very idea of the shâhid presupposes this ta’wîl, which is less a constructed interpretation than a spontaneous act, an inborn capacity. As for the beauty that qualifies this shâhid as a Witness of Contemplation, we must think both of Xvarnah, the Mazdean Light of Glory, and of Abû Shakûr’s testimony that the Manichaeans of Central Asia were particularly devoted to the worship of every beautiful being (see the study cited at the end of note 35 above). These are simply variations of the same experience. One variation is the theophanic perception of a beautiful face: to stand before the blaze of its beauty as Moses stood before the Burning Bush. Another is musical perception. Sufis who, like Rûzbehân, regularly took part in the spiritual concert (samâ’) clearly distinguished two kinds of listening, one sensual and the other spiritual. The latter presupposes a ta’wîl that is, so to speak, a priori: it occurs at the very moment of hearing. Yet puritans again denounce this as the practice of a zendîq. What is at stake, however, is listening to the inaudible, perceiving once again the ambiguity of appearance, the iltibâs. Toward the end of his life, Rûzbehân himself abstained from the samâ’, from gatherings of spiritual oratorio, and listened only to the sounds of a purely inward music. This long note aims at nothing more than suggesting the almost inexhaustible richness of the theme touched upon in Rûzbehân’s passing allusion. ↩

Jasmin, Chapter IV, §§ 51–52; see above, p. 90, note 103. Rûzbehân analyses these situations with extraordinary delicacy. He must also consider the case of Spirits who are not destined to “meet” and find one another on earth. Perhaps, he suggests, this belongs to that pre-eternal divine jealousy of love which, as the Book of the Clouding taught us, is ultimately the secret of a world upon which God “looks” or, conversely, “does not look.” But the mystical path of love, as Rûzbehân understands and has lived it, presupposes that Spirits “recognize one another” on earth. Without this mutual recognition, human love cannot fulfil its role of initiating the lover into divine love. ↩

Javânmard (§ 270) means not simply vir juvenis, a young man or adolescent, but a “knight of the soul,” a “spiritual knight.” The word expresses a characteristic Sufi ideal (Arabic fotowwat = Persian javânmardî). The ancient Iranians called themselves mard, in contrast to the Turanians: the man in the fullest sense, the hero, the superman. The term entered Iranian Sufism as a designation for the “spiritual hero,” the whole person, the free human being whom only Sufi spirituality can bring into being. In this sense, javân-mard is equivalent to mard, with the additional idea of youthfulness. See our Introduction au Jasmin, p. 119, note 164; earlier, Book II, Chapters IV and V; and below, vol. IV, Book VII, Chapter III. ↩

On these three modes of vision, see Jasmin, Chapter XXX, §§ 267–270. In his Tafsîr (’Arâ’is al-Bayân), Rûzbehân offers a beautiful spiritual interpretation of two Qur’anic verses. “Whoever contemplates my love for you within you will love you with my love for you” (on 19:96, vol. II, p. 18). “When He enveloped them in his light and clothed their innermost consciousness (asrâr) with the radiance of his love, they became adorned with every beauty, inwardly and outwardly. They are contemplated as a mirror of divine beauty; whoever sees them loves them. For God loves them, and they love him with his love. And creatures love them with the love God bears them, just as they love the lights of divine Beauty that they see within them” (on 20:39, vol. II, p. 31). ↩

Jasmin, Chapter XVIII, § 199. Just as Rûzbehân distinguished the faithful lovers from pious devotees in Chapter VIII, so throughout this chapter (§§ 194–201) he forcefully refutes the pretensions of libertine Sufis. They imagine that the condition of a faithful lover who is a malâmatî (one who accepts blame) is equivalent to simple rejection of religious and moral restraints, although they themselves cannot attain even the faintest theophanic perception. “Their inclination is nothing more than the stirring of their sensual passions. When they look at the outward form of beautiful beings, their eyes see nothing beyond that appearance. They see nothing of the beauty that results from a divine Operation, the colour that manifests a divine Attribute, the theophany of the Essence—all taking place in the cage of the human body without even coming from the Bird, the Spirit, that inhabits it. In short, they see none of these magnificent gifts that blossom at the outer limits of human existence ... They no longer distinguish the archetype from the idol. Yet they dare to claim: We are the daring men of our age, the men of paradoxes (Tammatîyân = Shattâhîyân; compare Hâfez, Dîwân, p. 257, no. 279: Tâmmat = shath), because we have made our home in the world of Omnipotence ... Beware of being seduced by the eloquence of these madmen (§§ 195–197).” Here, following certain autobiographical recollections, Rûzbehân reminds the faithful lovers that they must first pass through the Path of Trial and cross the bridge suspended over the hell of sensual nature (§ 201). Notice also that, for him, it is the perception of love’s pre-existent origin that lifts the veil before the Witness of Contemplation of the Uncreated (shâhid-e qidam). ↩

This final stage of vision is esoteric tawhîd. Far from dissolving into the formless, it brings forth before the mystic the form of the theophany suited to his particular experience—the prophetic vision “in the most beautiful of forms” (see above, p. 49, note 35). Rûzbehân’s Diwân bears witness to this by specifying each time the form in which the divine Friend appears to him. For “each divine Attribute has an eye, which is part of that Attribute itself, and it is through the Attribute’s own eye that the mystic contemplates that Attribute” (Risâla-ye Qodsîya, fol. 167b). We have already recalled (notes 91, 92, and 137) Rûzbehân’s care to place his theophanic understanding at an equal distance from belief in incarnation and abstract monotheism. Muslim writers on heresies and doctrines were far from sharing either his sensitivity to nuance or his sense of the necessary distinctions. An entire investigation remains to be made of those whom they indiscriminately placed in the category of holâliyân, believers in indwelling. ↩

See Gloss 210: “The unveiling of the divine eye, that is, the unveiling of the Beloved’s visible form for the mystics.” Hence, a few lines later, the mystic is introduced, brought forth, “into the vision of the Uncreated (dar ’ayn-e qidam)”: that is, the mystic sees created being as the divine eye sees it. Ibid., § 145. See above, p. 95, note 116, and p. 97, note 121. The point is therefore this: Abraham’s experience was still one of inward theophany; the time had not yet come for the prophet who would announce the theophany within created beauty. Rûzbehân has told us (§ 146) that if the eternal Bride had appeared to this spiritual prince in the features of human beauty, he would have suffered the fate of Moses on the mountain. Because Muhammad proclaimed the prophetic meaning of human beauty, he was the prophet of the religion of the faithful lovers: Sufism. “The masters of mystical gnosis know that a creature cannot bear the Uncreated in its pure state (§ 147).” Yet a creature could no more bear its vision within created beauty without the very discipline of the faithful lovers, which “initiates the disciple into discovering the rules of divine love through the experience of human love.” Only this path makes ultimate access possible to the highest and absolute vision, that of the elite of the elite. The circle closes: the theophanic perception of human beauty is no easy path. It is no more within a creature’s unaided powers than the pure vision of the Uncreated. Yet through the discipline of the faithful lovers, it opens as the only path leading toward that vision. ↩

Jasmin, Chapter XVII, §§ 187–188. The latter paragraph develops an astronomical symbolism related to Abraham’s experience (see above, p. 95, note 119, and p. 114, note 153). Mystics must eventually leave behind the planetary heavens. Like planets, they remain wanderers until they recognize the essence of the theophany. They must reach the Heaven of the Fixed Stars, which is the heaven of the divine Attribute, its constellations being the manifestations that determine the visible figures of the Attributes (see the preceding note). These forms are no longer experienced as something other than the One, but as the One’s own manifestation. Only the process of theophany, as the One’s multiplication by itself (1 × 1), saves us from shirk, the association of something else with the One (1 + 1). “Being then within God’s gaze”—that is, beings upon whom God looks, whose own gaze is God’s gaze (see Chapter III above)—“they repent of having associated these theophanies with Him [as though they were something other]. Their vision is so beautiful that they whisper in astonishment: Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:22). From these planetary stages, marked by Abraham’s cry, ‘This is my Lord’ (6:76–78), the Spirit journeys to the fixed constellations, to the theophanic manifestations that stud the Heaven of the divine Attributes. At the Orients of tawhîd, the rising stars of mystical experience point toward the world of the Uncreated and mark the path of initiation for the prisoners of what passes away. The theophany has nourished them, like a mother, with the milk of the divine Attribute in the world of divine election. For at the spiritual station designated by the verse, ‘It is toward you that I turn’ (7:142), the intelligence of the microcosm repeats in turn: ‘I am free from what you associate [with God]’ (6:19 and 78).” ↩

Light upon light: the eye with which God gazes upon himself. Hence the theme of the contemplative gaze (nazar) fixed upon the beauty of the shâhid, as a spiritual interpretation of the “Verse of Light” (see above, p. 84, note 87). Jasmin, Chapter VII, § 102: “Since the light of the Essence reveals itself in the light of the Operation [the process of theophany], we speak of Light upon Light (24:35). But this refers to a privilege belonging, among all created and time-bound beings, to the holy Spirits and the most sacred Intelligence (’Aql-e jalâlî = ’Aql-e qodsî), as it is written: God guides to his Light whom he wills (24:35) ... The more the lover’s contemplative gaze (nazar) discerns archetypal Beauty in the beloved’s attributes [and that, observes Gloss 89, is the whole purpose and substance of this chapter], the more his love increases. For the oil feeding the lamp of love has primordial Beauty as its source: the flame rises as this source grows, and sinks when it diminishes. For since the beginning of beginnings, love has been united with beauty.” Compare the statement Rûzbehân made in Shiraz during his first sermon, at the end of Chapter II above, and Suhrawardî’s Vade-mecum of the Faithful in Love (above, p. 84, note 87). ↩

On the difference between ’odhrîte love and “theophanic” love, see above, p. 91, note 106. Hellmut Ritter has admirably shown, in an additional appendix to his translation of I. J. Kratchkovski’s extended study, that Majnûn’s case cannot simply be assimilated to ’odhrîte love. It presents an essential difference that scholars have generally overlooked. See Die Frühgeschichte der Erzählung von Macnûn und Laila in der arabischen Literatur (Oriens, vol. 8, 1955, no. 1, pp. 1–50). ↩
